# Clinical Impact of 3- Vs. 5-Minute Delay and 30- Vs. 60-Second Intervals on Unattended Automated Office Blood Pressure Measurements

**Authors:** Erika E Lynn-Green; Jennifer L Cluett; Ruth-Alma N Turkson-Ocran; Kenneth J Mukamal; Jonathan X Li; Stephen P Juraschek

**Affiliations:** Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | Division of General Medicine, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | Healthcare Associates, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Guidelines advise automated office blood pressure (AOBP) with an initial 5-minute delay and multiple measurements at least 60 seconds apart. Recent studies suggest that AOBP may be accurate with shorter delays or intervals, but evidence in clinical settings is limited.

Patients referred to 1 hypertension (HTN) center underwent 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) and 1 of 4 nonrandomized, unattended AOBP protocols: a 3- or 5-minute delay with a 30- or 60-second interval, i.e., 3 min/30 s/30 s, 3/60/60, 5/30/30 and 5/60/60 protocols. HTN was defined as systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 or diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mm Hg.

We compared differences in mean blood pressure and HTN classification between average AOBP and awake-time ABPM by t-tests and Fisher’s exact test. Among 212 participants (mean 58.9 years, 61% women, 25% Black), there was substantial overlap in the probability distributions of awake-time ABPM and each of the 3 AOBP measures. SBP means were similar between the 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 protocols and 5/30/30 and 3/60/60 protocols. The 5/30/30 was associated with a higher proportion of systolic HTN, while the 3/60/60 protocol was associated with a higher proportion of diastolic HTN. There were no significant differences in systolic or diastolic HTN between 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 protocols with respect to awake-time ABPM.

In this quality improvement study, the shortest AOBP protocol did not differ significantly from the longest protocol. The time savings of shorter protocols may improve AOBP adoption in clinical practice without meaningfully compromising accuracy.

Blood pressure (BP) measurement is one of the most frequently performed clinical assessments, and the quality of measurement profoundly affects the detection and management of hypertension.1 The body of literature in support of hypertension screening and treatment is based on high-quality, standardized BP assessments.2,3 In particular, automated office BP (AOBP) with at least 2 measurements is increasingly recommended to improve both accuracy and precision in the clinic.4,5 However, to date, few outpatient clinics have adopted standardized AOBP protocols. One commonly cited barrier to implementing AOBP is the time required for patients to rest before and between replicate measures. We hypothesized that accurate and precise AOBP might be achieved with a shorter time delay and interval, but evidence is lacking.

Guidelines recommend an initial delay of 3–5 minutes before the first BP reading at a given visit6,7 with strong support from observational evidence showing profound changes in BP when taken later in the visit, presumably after the initial stimulus of arriving at the clinic has subsided.8 This was recently challenged by 2 randomized trials, showing that no rest before unattended AOBP more accurately reflected awake ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM),9 and yielded identical seated BP results to a 5-minute rest in an attended design.10 However, some have questioned the generalizability of these trials to clinical practice based on key departures from the typical patient experience, e.g., performing measurements after an informed consent process9 or conducting the study in a nonclinical setting with a standardized activity period.10

Current guidelines also recommend intervals of 1–2 minutes between AOBP readings7,11 based in part on trial protocols.9,10 While we recently reported that 30-second intervals yield equivalent results to 60-second intervals, this was only examined after a 5-minute delay.12 It is unclear if a reduced initial delay, in addition to shorter intervals between measurements, will have a greater impact on measurement accuracy. Along these lines, one study noted that the difference between the first and third measurements was most important for diagnosing hypertension, as these measurements are directly influenced by rest time and the duration of the measurement period.13

In this factorial design, quality improvement study performed in a general medicine hypertension clinic, our objectives were to compare patients’ mean awake-time ABPM with the mean of 3 AOBP measurements obtained (1) after a 3- vs. 5-minute delay or (2) with a 30- vs. 60-second pause between cuff deflation and the next inflation cycle. We hypothesized that the shortest AOBP protocol (i.e., a 3-minute delay with a 30-second pause) would be equivalent to the longest protocol (i.e., a 5-minute delay with a 60-second pause), and these effects would not differ by delay or pause interval (i.e., no interaction between the 2 factors).

## METHODS

### Population

We tested 2 different delay times with 2 different pause interval times for unattended AOBP among patients of the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) Hypertension Center at Healthcare Associates (where patients are referred for complex HTN management) between 15 April 2021 and 29 June 2023. As a quality improvement initiative, the BIDMC Institutional Review Board determined this project to be exempt research (see Supplementary Material 1 for details). The study began in the spring of 2021, with the plan to enroll 100 patients: 50 with a 5-minute delay and 60-second pause as an interval and 50 with a 3-minute delay and 60-second pause interval. In January 2022, in response to practice-wide changes to adopt a 30-second interval between BP measurements, the investigative team increased the scope of the quality improvement project to include an additional 100 patients using a 30-second pause interval (i.e., about 50 with a 5-minute delay and 30-second pause interval and 50 with a 3-minute delay and 30-second pause interval). Protocol was designated in advance by month, such that patients with appointments within a given month underwent the protocol assigned for that month. The final schedule for performing protocols may be found in Supplementary Table S1. Analyses were restricted to the patients (N = 212) who completed all BP assessments. Protocols were conducted using the SpaceLabs 90227 or 90217A-1 ABPM (Spacelabs Healthcare, Snoqualmie, WA) and the Omron HEM-907XL (Omron Healthcare, Lake Forest, IL), both with validation studies published previously.14

### Ambulatory BP measurement

Patients referred for ABPM underwent a standardized BP measurement protocol as follows. On day 1, patients were brought to a private exam room where a tape measure was used to measure the circumference of their mid-arm to determine cuff size; when available, cuff sizes were confirmed using the range indicators printed on the cuff (Spacelabs or Omron). BP measurements were performed using the nondominant arm unless there was a medical contraindication such as tremor, prior mastectomy, or continuous blood glucose monitor.

Patients were then fitted for ABPM, which they wore for the following 25 hours. Patients then took off the monitor and returned the device 1–2 days later during a follow-up visit. ABPMs were preprogrammed to measure BP every 20 minutes during awake hours and hourly during sleep hours based on patients’ self-reported sleep/wake times. When the device was actively measuring, patients were asked to remain still and let their arm rest on their other arm, on an adjacent table, or at heart level. Participants were given a log for sleep times, awake times, and relevant activities (such as exercise, meals, timing of medications, driving time, and periods when the monitor was removed) during the 25-hour period. The actual sleep and awake times were used to determine the average awake ABPM. The majority of participants had over 20 successful awake ABPM readings. Notably, there were only 2 patients with less than 20 measurements while awake (N = 18 and 19, respectively).15

### Unattended AOBP measurement

Unattended AOBP readings were performed every time during the visit when the ABPM device was returned (day 2 or 3, depending on the date of ABPM placement). An additional day between ABPM and AOBP measurements was introduced due to an unrelated clinic schedule change on 16 May 2022. No changes were made to patients’ hypertension medication regimen from the 7 days prior to the ABPM monitoring period through the follow-up visit in the clinic. Patients were assigned to 1 of 4 AOBP timing protocols by month based on a prespecified schedule (Supplementary Table S1): 5-minute delay and 60-second pause intervals (N = 67, “5/60/60”), 3-minute delay and 60-second pause intervals (N = 51, “3/60/60”), 5-minute delay and 30-second pause intervals (N = 50, “5/30/30”), 3-minute delay and 30-second pause intervals (N = 44, “3/30/30”).

Patients underwent an unattended, preprogrammed 3- or 5-minute delay followed by 3 BP measurements (designated M0–M2), separated by a 30- or 60-second pause interval. Before measurement, clinic staff were trained to position patients with their feet on the floor, backs supported, palms facing upright, and cuffs placed on bare skin. Arms were elevated at heart level and supported on a table. Signage was posted outside the clinic room to minimize noise and interruptions. The monitor display did not display BP readings during measurements. Staff left the room after starting the monitor and returned after the third measurement was complete.

We defined stage 2 or uncontrolled hypertension as a systolic blood pressure (SBP) ≥140 mm Hg and/or diastolic Blood pressure (BP) (DBP) ≥90 mm Hg, following the National Committee for Quality Assurance’s Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set definition for uncontrolled BP. Compliance with this metric is used as a benchmark for quality, linked to financial incentives for clinical practices. This definition was of primary interest to our clinic in this quality improvement project.

### Other covariates

Demographic information on age, sex, and race were obtained from the medical record. As part of clinical care, patients were asked about prior diagnoses of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, sleep apnea, current antihypertensive and cholesterol-lowering medications, smoking status, and alcohol use. The most recent available data on body mass index and creatinine were obtained from the medical record. We also tracked patients’ reason(s) for referral (new diagnosis of hypertension, uncontrolled hypertension, white coat hypertension, orthostatic symptoms, or other).

### Statistical analysis

Population-level characteristics were assessed using both overall means and proportions and according to the 4 protocols. Bland–Altman plots were used to visualize differences between the mean AOBP by protocol. We calculated the mean and SD for SBP and DBP by measurement type according to each protocol, as well as the prevalence of stage 2 or uncontrolled hypertension (SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg) according to each protocol. All means and proportions used mean awake-time ABPM as a reference. Means were compared using paired t-tests and reported as mean differences; proportions were compared using the McNemar χ2 test. Root-mean-square errors were determined for each measurement. We produced Lowess curves and scatter plots displaying the means of AOBP and ABPM for every patient by date of visit to evaluate any trends over time given the clinic setting (Supplementary Figure S1).

We calculated differences between each AOBP measurement and awake-time ABPM, using generalized estimating equations (normal family, identity link, robust variance estimator) to model the mean value at each measurement. We also examined how differences in measurements differed by protocol. In addition, we determined the performance of the distinct protocols for identifying patients with SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg via area of the curve, sensitivity, specificity, positive likelihood ratio, and negative likelihood ratio. This was repeated in supplemental analyses for SBP ≥130 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥80 mm Hg.

We also used linear regression to examine the association of the 4 AOBP protocols with each BP measurement adjusted for age, sex, and race (model 1) or additionally adjusted for the difference between the first automated measurement and awake-time ABPM in Supplemental analyses (model 2). In addition, we examined whether the association between each measurement and awake-time ABPM differed across each study protocol compared to the 5/60/60 protocol via protocol-by-BP measurement interaction terms adjusted for age, sex, and race (model 1) or additionally adjusted for the difference between the first automated measurement and awake-time ABPM in supplemental analyses (model 2) as described above. These comparisons were repeated using logistic regression with respect to the classification of stage 2 or uncontrolled hypertension (SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg). In sensitivity analyses, we reanalyzed data by factorial design (3- vs. 5-minute delay or 30- vs. 60-second interval) due to the presence of an interaction between delay and intervals.

All statistical analyses were performed using Stata 15.1 (StataCorp LP, College Station, TX). A 2-tailed P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

## RESULTS

### Population characteristics

Of 218 participating patients, 212 completed the protocol and were included in analyses with 61% women, 25% Black patients, and a mean age of 58.9 years (Table 1). The majority (82%) of patients were referred for management of hypertension (new diagnosis, uncontrolled disease, or white coat). Patient characteristics were similar across all 4 individual protocols (Table 1) and factorial design (Supplementary Table S2).

### Average BP

For SBP, patient-specific means were similar between the 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 protocols as well as between the 5/30/30 and 3/60/60 protocols (Figure 1). Average awake-time ABPM was 129.0 ± 14/78.0 ± 10 for the 5/60/60 protocol, 129.7 ± 14/75.0 ± 10 for the 3/60/60 protocol, 129.0 ± 13/77.3 ± 11 for the 5/30/30 protocol, and 130.2 ± 12/77.9 ± 9 for the 3/30/30 protocol (Table 2). Bland–Altman plots did not reveal differential bias or precision across the mean BP values (Supplementary Figure S2). The performance of the different protocols was similar, without clear evidence that any single protocol was better for identifying awake-time hypertension on APBM (Supplementary Tables S3 and S4).

The 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 protocols performed similarly, with nonsignificant differences between mean AOBP and mean awake-time ABPM for SBP (1.3 mm Hg, P = 0.46; 0.9 mm Hg, P = 0.69, respectively) and DBP (0.5 mm Hg, P = 0.62; −0.4 mm Hg, P = 0.78, respectively) (Table 2). Other protocols showed a significant difference between mean AOBP and mean awake-time ABPM for SBP (7.0 mm Hg, P = 0.004 for 3/60/60; 6.7 mm Hg, P < 0.01 for 5/30/30), though not for DBP (1.9 mm Hg, P = 0.15 for 3/60/60; 2.4 mm Hg, P = 0.07 for 5/30/30). Differences in BP measures (M1 vs. M0, M2 vs. M1, or M2 vs. M1) did not differ by protocol (Supplementary Table S5).

### Proportion with hypertension

There were no significant differences in systolic or diastolic HTN (i.e., SBP ≥140 mm Hg and/or DBP ≥90 mm Hg) between 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 protocols with respect to awake-time ABPM. Compared to awake-time ABPM, there were significant differences in the proportion with systolic HTN observed with the 5/30/30 protocol (26%, P = 0.002) and in the proportion with diastolic HTN with the 3/60/60 protocol (11.8%, P = 0.03) (Table 2; for comparisons of means of SBP and DBP, see Supplementary Table S6).

Compared to 5/60/60, the 3/60/60 and 5/30/30 protocols were associated with higher odds of systolic hypertension (average M0–M2 OR of 2.3 [95% CI: 1.0, 5.4], and 2.7 [95% CI: 1.2, 6.3], respectively) (Table 3). There were no significant differences in the odds of hypertension between the 3/30/30 and the 5/60/60 protocols.

### Factorial analysis

There was evidence of interaction by delay and interval protocols in relation to SBP for the first AOBP measurement; thus, we examined factorial contrasts in sensitivity analyses. Baseline characteristics were generally balanced across factors (Supplementary Table S2). Moreover, measurement distributions and means were roughly similar between the 5- and 3-minute delays and the 60- and 30-second intervals for both SBP and DBP (Supplementary Figures S3 and S4; Supplementary Table S8). There was no evidence that a 3- vs. 5-minute delay or a 30- vs. 60-second interval was associated with higher odds of hypertension (Supplementary Table S9). Moreover, there was no evidence that AOBP measurements (individually or averaged) associated with awake-time ABPM differently across factors (Supplementary Table S10).

## DISCUSSION

This quality improvement study of over 200 patients investigated the real-world performance of various unattended AOBP protocols in a clinic setting compared to awake-time ABPM. Overall, our results indicate that the shortest AOBP protocol, with a 3-minute initial delay and 30-second pause intervals between measurements, was statistically equivalent to the longest protocol with a 5-minute delay and 60-second intervals. Moreover, there were no major differences in the associations between individual AOBP measurements and awake-time ABPM regardless of delay and interval settings.

AOBP is an important tool for high-quality BP measurements in the clinic setting, which remains a crucial environment for diagnosing and managing hypertension.4,16 However, AOBP uptake has been low, motivating inquiry into whether a shortened time interval might yield BP measures with similar accuracy and precision as longer AOBP protocols used in prominent clinical trials.17,18

Recent randomized trials showed that a shorter delay compared to a 5-minute delay had no impact on BP measurements.9,10 However, one of these trials was attended in a research environment,10 in which BP measurements are known to differ from clinic environments.19 While the other trial was performed unattended in a clinic setting, patients underwent a consent process prior to participation, which likely entailed a semi-rested period in the seated position.9 Many describe the logistic challenges and rush to appointments as a stressful patient experience that may alter BP. One large study showed significant reductions in BP between the first and second BP measurements in the clinic.8 In contrast, our study was performed in a typical office setting with usual intake procedures.

The longest protocol, 5/60/60, had average SBP and DBP AOBP readings that did not significantly differ from the shortest protocol, 3/30/30. This was true for each individual AOBP measurement (M0, M1, and M2) as well as for the mean of M1 and M2 (excluding the first reading) and the overall mean of all 3 readings. Furthermore, the shortest protocol did not compromise the accuracy of BP measurement compared to the longest protocol. In hypertension classification, the proportion of patients with an AOBP mean SBP over 140 mm Hg or DBP over 90 mm Hg who had an ABPM mean under these cutoffs also did not significantly differ between the longest and shortest protocols. This was consistent across both the absolute proportions of hypertension classification compared to ABPM and for the odds of classifying a patient as hypertensive compared to the longest protocol.

Multiple guidelines recommend 1–2 minutes between BP measurements20,21 based on a few studies showing minimal differences between 1- and 2-minute intervals.22,23 However, data comparing measurements with shorter time intervals are limited. Imamura and colleagues found similar performance between measurements with 30- and 60-second intervals.24 Our previous work in a distinct group of over 100 patients found that a 30-second interval was statistically equivalent to 60 seconds in the clinic setting following a 5-minute delay.12 The present study examined this question after a 3-minute delay, showing similar accuracy and precision between shorter and longer intervals regardless of the initial delay. Another important consideration is the sequence effect, which has been well-described and has been a major rationale behind discarding the first measurement when assessing BP.25–27 Later measures may be especially influenced by a shorter interval. Nevertheless, we did not observe consistent differences across protocol assignments even after discarding the first measurement.

In our analysis, an interaction effect between delay and interval was present with respect to SBP from the first AOBP measure, affecting the factorial analysis; however, the reasons for this are unclear and were potentially by chance. This is supported by the observation that an interaction involving measurement 1, could not be influenced by the pause interval. In addition, a close examination of protocol assignments did not reveal any consistent pattern of bias. In fact, the most discordant pairings, 5/30/30 and 3/60/60 as well as 5/60/60 and 3/30/30 were the most alike. These differences were likely not physiologic but should be the focus of further work.

This study has limitations. First, patients were not randomized in our study but were assigned to an AOBP protocol a priori on a month-by-month basis, possibly introducing confounding factors not accounted for between groups. Nevertheless, baseline characteristics were balanced across the 4 protocols. Second, practice staff and procedures changed over time. As the interval comparison was added later in the 2-year study period, there could be temporal effects on measurement performance and the patient population. However, to account for this, we intentionally repeated the 5/60/60 assessment throughout the study. Moreover, the means of AOBP and ABPM were reassuringly consistent across the study period. Third, while our study included over 200 people, no power calculations were performed prior to the study’s commencement, and therefore, the findings should not be interpreted as definitive. It should also be noted that there may be differences and variability in the training and implementation of AOBP by staff, which could reduce our ability to detect differences. Nevertheless, fluctuation in staff training and practice is reflective of real-world settings. Fourth, it is possible that performing AOBP after ABPM would lead to an order effect as patients would be acclimated to BP readings, although AOBP readings were still higher than ABPM on average, and this order effect was consistent across the protocols. Nevertheless, randomizing patients into distinct orders would allow for a better comparison of AOBP to ABPM. Fifth, the clinical importance of attended vs. unattended BP measurements is an ongoing debate; it is unclear whether our results might differ when attended.28–30 Sixth, our study looked at both BP measurement and the classification of BP ≥140/≥90 mm Hg. While measurement did not differ consistently between protocols, the traditional approach classified adults with BP ≥140/≥90 mm Hg most similarly to ABPM. It is possible that devices may perform differently at different ranges of BP, which should be a focus of subsequent work. Seventh, we were not able to examine the effects of medication use and did not collect details of concurrent antihypertensive class as part of this study, which should be examined. Last, BP variability between visits is greater than measurements within-visit.31 The impact of a shorter within-visit protocol on between-visit BP variability remains an important question for subsequent research. Nevertheless, the discordance between AOBP and awake-time ABPM observed in our study supports recommendations to base clinical decisions on more than one visit, as within-person differences are not the same as group differences.

Our study has clinical implications for providers taking BP measurements in outpatient settings and potential implications for guidelines related to AOBP. AOBP was very similar to awake-time ABPM, demonstrating the value of this form of measurement in the clinic setting. However, the adoption of AOBP, already recommended for BP measurement quality improvement, has been limited in part due to concerns related to perceived time requirements. In our investigation, measurement accuracy and precision did not differ significantly between the longest (7 minutes) and the shortest protocols (4 minutes). Three minutes of rest time saved per patient is substantial for busy clinic environments. Time savings with similar accuracy suggested by these findings could promote AOBP uptake and optimal BP measurement for every clinic patient. Importantly, our findings reinforce reports from recent trials9,10 that a shortened rest period is acceptable for AOBP without compromising its accuracy in a real-world context, addressing concerns about the generalizability of these prior works to clinical care.

In conclusion, while several areas remain to be further investigated, in this clinic-based quality improvement study, the shortest AOBP protocol reduced time without compromising BP measurement accuracy or HTN classification compared to the longest protocol. These results support the implementation of more time-efficient AOBP in clinical practice.
